segments.text: Scientists just released the biggest ever map of a fruit fly's brain. It could help us understand our own minds one day. This is Models & Agents for Beginners, Episode 162. A Google Research Group teamed up with scientists at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, or HHMI. Together they published a wiring diagram of a male fruit fly's whole brain and nervous system. A wiring diagram is just a chart of every cable-like link that carries a signal from one cell

to another. This chart covers over 166,000 nerve cells, called neurons. It also covers 125 million connections between those cells. The map runs from the head all the way down a nerve cord that works like a spinal cord.

Picture the full blueprint of a giant city, every highway, alley, and traffic light included. Now swap the streets for the actual paths neurons used to talk to each other. That is the kind of chart they just released.

It is the largest brain map so far if you count neurons that humans have already checked by hand. That checking step is called proofreading, which means a person looks at the computer's tracing and confirms each link is real.
Earlier charts only covered part of a female fly's brain, and they held far fewer details. Researchers now have a male version and a female version they can set side by side.

Think of two editions of the same city's atlas, printed years apart, so you can circle what changed. A 2020 project called HHMI brain mapped just 25,000 neurons and 20 million connections in a portion of a female fly's brain.
Comparing the new chart with that older one lets scientists spot exact structural differences. Those differences might help explain why males and females act differently in certain ways.

Nervous systems across animals share surprising similarities. Studying these smaller maps with artificial intelligence, or AI, lets researchers practice techniques they can later use on bigger, more complex brains.
The same effort now extends to mapping smaller organisms such as fish, which build skill for later human related studies.
Work like this could eventually lead to better tools for treating conditions that affect how people think and feel.
It also shows AI as a partner in scientific discovery, not only as something that writes essays or answers homework questions.
There is not a public demo you can click through yet. You can follow the Google Research and HHMI Janelia teams on X and watch the updates they post as they learn more from the map.
They do not scan a living fly the way your phone scans a face. If you have ever watched someone cut a loaf into thin slices so they can see every layer inside, you already understand the first move.
Scientists cut the brain into thousands of extremely thin sheets, then take a very detailed photo of each sheet.
Next, AI software studies those photos and decides which tiny specs belong to the same long twisting neuron.
That matching job is like assembling a huge three-dimensional puzzle, except every piece is a faint branch or a contact point.
After the software joins the pieces, people check the work by hand, which is the proofreading step from the announcement.
The finished chart shows exactly which neurons link to which others and how strong those links are.
Actions begin with those links. If two groups of neurons chatter more than they should or less, an animal's behavior can change.
By making these charts for simpler creatures first, scientists get better at the whole process before they try larger brains.
The AI does the heavy lifting of tracing millions of tiny lines, and humans make sure the final map is accurate.
Once you see it as careful tracing plus a human double check, the whole thing clicks into place.

Coursera just published a free beginners guide that walks through what AI agents are, and how regular people can start experimenting with them.
An AI agent is a software helper that can carry out a task without you steering every single click.
The guide uses everyday language and includes short videos plus interactive steps you can follow on a laptop or a phone.
It covers the basic ideas behind agents that can answer questions or organize information on their own.
Think of a reliable classmate who can finish a checklist while you work on something else.
Go to Coursera's website, open their article on how to build AI agents, and start with the first section.
It takes about 15 to 20 minutes, and gives you clear next actions you can try right away.
